pos: n. (an idiom for the pupil of the eye, and so the most tenderly guarded thing)
etymology: Hebrew ishon, the little man, the pupil — so called from the tiny figure reflected in it — and in Deuteronomy 32:10 babah, the gate or apple of the eye. The English apple was the old word for the pupil, from its round shape.
biblical_def: The apple of the eye is the pupil, and in the Authorized Version it is the standing figure for what a man guards most instinctively and most absolutely. The Hebrew behind it in Psalm 17 is ishon, the little man, named for the small reflected figure a man sees looking into another's eye. Moses applies it to God's keeping of Israel in the wilderness: “he led him about, he instructed him, he kept him as the apple of his eye” (Deuteronomy 32:10). David turns it into a prayer: “Keep me as the apple of the eye, hide me under the shadow of thy wings” (Psalm 17:8). Zechariah makes it a threat against the nations: “he that toucheth you toucheth the apple of his eye” (Zechariah 2:8). And Solomon applies it to the law itself: “Keep my commandments, and live; and my law as the apple of thine eye” (Proverbs 7:2). The force of the figure is in the reflex. No man deliberates about protecting his eye; the lid closes before the mind consults. That is the kind of keeping God is said to exercise over His people, and that is the kind of regard His people are commanded to have for His word. The doctrine is preservation, and it is not sentiment but instinct raised to omnipotence.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): Apple of the eye, the pupil; figuratively, that which is dearest and most carefully guarded, as God keeps His people and as His people are to keep His law.
webster_full: Hebrew ishon, the little man, the pupil, from the small figure reflected in it.
In Deuteronomy 32:10, Hebrew babah, the gate or apple of the eye.
The old English apple meant the pupil, from its round shape.

Used of the law to be kept by the believer, Proverbs 7:2.

corruption_summary: The figure is reduced to a term of fond endearment, when in Scripture it carries the doctrine of God's effectual preservation of His elect.
corruption_paragraphs: In ordinary speech the apple of one's eye has become a mild compliment paid to a favourite child, and the softening is not harmless when the phrase is read back into Scripture. Deuteronomy 32:10 is not a sentiment about fondness; it is a statement about a keeping that held a stubborn nation together through forty years of a waste howling wilderness that would otherwise have killed them. Zechariah 2:8 is not affectionate at all. It is a warning that to touch this people is to put a finger in the eye of the LORD of hosts.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the perseverance of the saints as God's work rather than the believer's achievement. The eye is kept by a lid that moves faster than thought, and the comparison is deliberate: those whom the Father has given to the Son are guarded by a vigilance that does not sleep, deliberate, or weigh the cost. The same verse that asks to be kept as the apple of the eye asks next to be hidden under the shadow of His wings, and the two figures together are a complete doctrine of preservation.

pos: n. (the unleavened bread of the passover; also a prisoner's ration)
etymology: Hebrew lechem oni, bread of affliction or of poverty, from lechem, bread, and oni, affliction, humiliation, poverty, from anah, to be bowed down. Named three times in the Authorized Version.
biblical_def: The bread of affliction is the unleavened bread of the passover, eaten for seven days as a memorial of the haste and the misery of the departure from Egypt: “Thou shalt eat no leavened bread with it; seven days shalt thou eat unleavened bread therewith, even the bread of affliction; for thou camest forth out of the land of Egypt in haste” (Deuteronomy 16:3). The reason given is remembrance. Flat, poor, unrisen bread was put into the mouth of every Israelite once a year so that a people who would soon be prosperous in a land flowing with milk and honey could not forget what they had been and who had brought them out. The phrase has a second and harsher use: it is the prison ration ordered for the prophet Micaiah by Ahab, who told his officer to feed him with bread of affliction and water of affliction until the king came back in peace — and the king did not come back in peace. The two uses belong together. The appointed bread of affliction is a sacrament of memory; the bread of affliction a king forces on a true prophet is persecution. In both, poor bread is the mark of those who belong to God in a world not yet put right.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): Bread of affliction, the unleavened bread of the passover, eaten in memory of the haste and misery of the exodus; also the scant ration given to a prisoner.

corruption_summary: Remembrance is treated as a mood to be summoned rather than a practice to be kept; Scripture appointed a taste, a date and a week for it.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern habit is to regard remembering as an inward act, generated by sincerity when the occasion calls for it. Scripture is far less trusting of the memory than that. It appointed a food, a season and a duration, and made the remembering physical: seven days of flat bread, tasted by children who would ask why. The parallel for the church is the Lord's Supper, which is likewise not a feeling but a practice with elements, and which likewise encodes an affliction — broken bread — in the middle of a people's prosperity.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God teaches His people through appointed signs, and that prosperity is the condition under which remembrance is most likely to fail. Deuteronomy 16 was given to a generation about to stop being slaves. The bread of affliction was not nostalgia for Egypt; it was protection against the forgetfulness that comes with milk and honey, and the warning stands over every comfortable congregation that has not tasted anything poor in years.

pos: n. (the cup of God's wrath, which staggers those who drink it)
etymology: Hebrew kos ha-tarelah, the cup of reeling or staggering, from kos, a cup, and tarelah, reeling, staggering as a drunken man. Named three times in the Authorized Version.
biblical_def: The cup of trembling is the cup of God's wrath, and the Hebrew behind trembling is tarelah, reeling — the stagger of a man who has drunk too much. Isaiah sets it in the hand of Jerusalem under judgment: “Awake, awake, stand up, O Jerusalem, which hast drunk at the hand of the LORD the cup of his fury; thou hast drunken the dregs of the cup of trembling, and wrung them out” (Isaiah 51:17). The dregs are the bitterest part, settled at the bottom, and Jerusalem has drained to them and wrung the vessel out. Then comes one of the great reversals in the prophets: “Behold, I have taken out of thine hand the cup of trembling, even the dregs of the cup of my fury; thou shalt no more drink it again” (Isaiah 51:22). The cup is not emptied by the sinner's endurance; it is taken out of the hand. Where it goes is settled in Gethsemane, where the Son asks whether this cup may pass, and then takes it: the cup the Father gives Him is the cup He had taken out of His people's hand. Substitution is the doctrine, and the figure is exact. Someone drank the dregs. It was not Jerusalem.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): Cup of trembling, the cup of divine wrath, which makes the drinker reel and stagger; taken out of Jerusalem's hand by the LORD, and drunk by Christ.

corruption_summary: Divine wrath is recast as a natural consequence rather than a cup God gives; the figure in Isaiah is of a cup handed over, taken away, and drunk by another.
corruption_paragraphs: The dominant evangelical correction of the last generation has been to redefine wrath as consequence — sin's own built-in result, with God merely declining to intervene. Isaiah 51 will not bear it. The cup is drunk at the hand of the LORD; it is His fury, He gives it, and He takes it back. Consequence has no hand. The motive for the softening is pastoral, and the cost is the atonement, because a wrath that nobody pours is a wrath nobody needs to bear, and Gethsemane becomes incomprehensible.

Open theism and process theology press the same point further, denying that God can be said to visit wrath at all without compromising His love. The dictionary answers with the text: the same chapter that describes the cup describes the God who pleadeth the cause of his people, and it is His love that takes the cup out of their hand. The two are not in competition. Christ asked in the garden whether the cup might pass from Him, and then drank it to the dregs, and that is the only account of divine love the New Testament gives.

pos: n. pl. (the inexhaustible springs from which the redeemed draw)
etymology: Hebrew mayenei ha-yeshuah, the springs of salvation, from mayan, a spring or fountain, from ayin, an eye — a spring being the eye of the earth — with yeshuah, salvation. The phrase occurs once in the Authorized Version.
biblical_def: The wells of salvation appear once, at the end of Isaiah's song of the redeemed: “Therefore with joy shall ye draw water out of the wells of salvation” (Isaiah 12:3). The Hebrew is mayan, not a cistern but a living spring, and the word is built on ayin, an eye, because a spring is the eye of the earth where water looks out. Three things are given in the one verse. The water is drawn, which means salvation is appropriated and not merely admired — there is a bucket and an arm in the picture. It is drawn with joy, which makes gladness the proper manner of the Christian life and not an optional temperament. And the source is wells in the plural, springs that do not fail, because what is drawn from them was never the drawer's to begin with. Isaiah 12 is a song appointed for a day of restoration, sung by a people who had been under the cup of trembling and had it taken out of their hand. Our Lord takes the figure up at the feast of tabernacles, at the very moment the water was being drawn and poured in the temple, and stands and cries that the thirsty should come to Him and drink, and that out of the believer's belly shall flow rivers of living water.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): Wells of salvation, the living springs of God's saving mercy, from which the redeemed draw with joy; Hebrew mayan, a spring, from ayin, an eye.

corruption_summary: Salvation is treated as a transaction completed and shelved, rather than a spring to be drawn from daily and with gladness.
corruption_paragraphs: Two errors are answered by the one verse. The first treats salvation as a single past transaction, filed and finished, so that the believer has nothing left to do with it but remember the date. Isaiah puts a bucket in his hand and tells him to draw. The second is the opposite error of the sacramental systems, which make the well a cistern under the church's management, so that grace is dispensed by an institution rather than drawn by the thirsty. Mayan is a spring, not a reservoir, and springs are not administered.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the duty and the gladness of appropriation. The means of grace — the word read and preached, prayer, the ordinances, the assembly of the saints — are the buckets, and a Christian who owns a well and never lowers anything into it will be thirsty in the middle of plenty. Isaiah says the drawing is done with joy, which is the note most commonly missing. A dutiful, joyless drawing has misread the verse by half.

word: Brand Plucked Out of the Fire
pronunciation: BRAND PLUKT owt uv the FYRE
pos: n. (a figure for one rescued from imminent destruction by sheer mercy)
etymology: Hebrew ud mutsal me-esh, a brand snatched from fire, from ud, a firebrand or charred stick, and natsal, to snatch away or deliver. The phrase occurs once in the Authorized Version, Zechariah 3:2.
biblical_def: A brand plucked out of the fire is a charred stick snatched from a blaze before it is consumed, and Scripture uses it for a sinner rescued by mercy alone. The great instance is Zechariah's vision of Joshua the high priest standing before the angel in filthy garments, with Satan at his right hand to resist him: “And the LORD said unto Satan, The LORD rebuke thee, O Satan; even the LORD that hath chosen Jerusalem rebuke thee: is not this a brand plucked out of the fire?” (Zechariah 3:2). Everything in the scene is against Joshua. The accusation is true, the garments are filthy, and he says not one word in his own defence. The answer to Satan is not that Joshua is better than he looks. It is election — the LORD that hath chosen Jerusalem — and it is rescue: this man is a brand, already burnt, pulled out by a hand that reached into the fire. Amos uses the same figure of a people who were snatched and did not return. The brand has no merit and no beauty; it is black and it smells of smoke, and the only thing to be said for it is that it is out. That is the doctrine of justification put in one image, and the next verse removes the filthy garments and clothes him with change of raiment.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): A brand plucked out of the fire, a charred stick snatched from burning; figuratively, a sinner rescued from destruction by sovereign mercy, as Joshua the high priest in Zechariah 3.
webster_full: Hebrew ud, a firebrand, a charred stick from the hearth.

corruption_summary: Rescue is recast as rehabilitation, as though the brand were improved rather than snatched; the text gives it no merit and no defence.
corruption_paragraphs: The therapeutic retelling of Zechariah 3 makes Joshua a man with low self-esteem whom God affirms, and the filthy garments a metaphor for shame that needs reframing. The text is about guilt, not shame, and Satan's accusation is not a lie that needs correcting but a truth that needs answering. It is answered by election and by substitution: the garments are not explained away, they are taken off and replaced. A gospel that reassures the brand about its charring has not got it out of the fire.

The Roman and synergist readings fail at the other end. If Joshua contributes anything, the figure collapses, because a brand in a fire contributes nothing but combustibility. Zechariah gives the whole transaction to the LORD who chose Jerusalem, and gives Joshua no speech at all. The dictionary holds the monergistic reading because the image permits no other: wood does not pull itself out of a fire.

pos: n. pl. (our Lord's figure for hypocrites, fair without and foul within)
etymology: From whited, whitewashed, the old past participle of white as a verb; rendering Greek taphoi kekoniamenoi, tombs plastered with lime, from konia, dust or lime. The phrase occurs once in the Authorized Version.
biblical_def: Whited sepulchres is our Lord's name for the scribes and Pharisees in the sixth of the seven woes: “Woe unto you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! for ye are like unto whited sepulchres, which indeed appear beautiful outward, but are within full of dead men's bones, and of all uncleanness” (Matthew 23:27). The image is drawn from a real practice. Tombs around Jerusalem were whitewashed with lime, partly for appearance and partly as a warning, because contact with a grave made a Jew ceremonially unclean for seven days — so the white was a sign saying keep off. Our Lord turns the sign inside out. The whitewash that was meant to warn has become a disguise; the fair outside now conceals rather than announces the death within. In Luke He presses it harder still and calls them graves which appear not, over which men walk unawares, so that the defilement spreads to those who never knew they were near a tomb — which is exactly the harm a hypocritical ministry does to a congregation. The charge is not that these men were irreligious. They were scrupulous, tithing their herbs. The charge is that the religion was all surface, and that beneath the lime there was nothing alive.

corruption_summary: Hypocrisy is redefined as the gap between stated ideals and private failure, which makes every sincere Christian a hypocrite and leaves the real thing unnamed.
corruption_paragraphs: The commonest modern use of hypocrite is to mean anyone whose practice falls short of his profession, and on that definition every Christian who has ever confessed sin qualifies. The word is then used to silence the church: you have no standing to call anything sin, because you sin. Our Lord's usage is narrower and far more serious. The Pharisees were not men striving and failing; they were men content with the lime. The hypocrite is not the believer who falls short of the standard he upholds but the man who has substituted the appearance of righteousness for the pursuit of it.

The second corruption runs the other way, among the scrupulous: a reading that makes the woe fall on external religion as such, so that order, discipline, careful obedience and tithing become suspect. Our Lord explicitly refuses that inference in the same discourse — these ought ye to have done, and not to leave the other undone. The outside is to be washed too. The fault was never that the Pharisees kept the outside clean; it was that they thought that was all there was, and the dead men's bones stayed where they were.

pos: n. (our Lord's figure for the impossibility of a rich man saving himself)
etymology: Greek trupema rhaphidos in Matthew, trumalia rhaphidos in Mark, the hole or perforation of a sewing needle; Luke has trumalias belones, a surgeon's needle. Named in all three synoptic Gospels.
biblical_def: The eye of a needle is our Lord's measure of impossibility, spoken immediately after the rich young ruler went away sorrowful: “And again I say unto you, It is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle, than for a rich man to enter into the kingdom of God” (Matthew 19:24). Mark repeats it in the same words and Luke gives it with a surgeon's needle, the finest then known. The disciples understood it exactly as it sounds — they were exceedingly amazed and asked who then can be saved — and our Lord did not soften it. He answered that with men this is impossible, but with God all things are possible, which is the point of the saying and the reason it must not be blunted. The popular explanation that the Needle's Eye was a small gate in Jerusalem through which a camel could pass on its knees has no ancient evidence whatever and first appears many centuries later; it was invented to make the camel merely difficult instead of impossible. That ruins the doctrine. Our Lord chose the largest beast in Palestine and the smallest hole in common use because He meant a thing that cannot be done, and then located the possibility in God alone. Salvation is not hard for the rich. It is impossible for anyone, and God does it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): Eye of a needle, the perforation of a sewing needle; used by Christ as a figure of absolute impossibility, a camel being the largest beast and the needle's eye the smallest opening.

corruption_summary: The saying is defused by a legend about a camel gate, turning an impossibility into an inconvenience and emptying the answer our Lord gave.
corruption_paragraphs: The most persistent corruption of this text is the pulpit tradition that the eye of the needle was a low postern gate in the Jerusalem wall, so that a camel could squeeze through by being unloaded and made to kneel — from which preachers draw a lesson about humility and letting go of possessions. There is no evidence for such a gate in any ancient source, and the explanation is not attested until long after the New Testament era. It is an invention, and its effect is to replace an impossibility with a difficulty, which is precisely the move the disciples did not make and our Lord did not permit.

The second corruption, from the opposite direction, is the ascetic reading that makes wealth itself damning and poverty meritorious, as though the camel could pass by being poor. Our Lord says the impossibility is general: the disciples ask who then can be saved, not which rich man. Abraham, Job and Joseph of Arimathaea were wealthy men and are not in hell. What damns is trust in riches, and the remedy is not redistribution but regeneration, which only God performs.

pos: n. (Christ's resurrection as the pledge and pattern of the saints' rising)
etymology: Greek aparche ton kekoimemenon, the firstfruit of those fallen asleep, from aparche, the first portion of a harvest offered to God, and koimao, to fall asleep — the New Testament's ordinary word for a believer's death.
biblical_def: The phrase occurs once, as the hinge of the great resurrection chapter: “But now is Christ risen from the dead, and become the firstfruits of them that slept” (1 Corinthians 15:20). Paul draws on the law of firstfruits, where the first sheaf of a harvest was brought to the LORD and the rest of the field followed it into the barn. The firstfruits are not a sample of what might happen; they are the first instalment of a harvest already begun, and the farmer who has brought in the sheaf is not speculating about the crop. So Christ's rising is neither a solitary marvel nor a symbol of hope in general. It is the first of a series, and the series is His people. The word for their death is slept, which Paul uses deliberately throughout the chapter and which the church has kept in the word cemetery, a sleeping-place. He adds the order a few verses later: Christ the firstfruits, afterward they that are Christ's at his coming. The doctrine is bodily resurrection, in that order and on that ground, and Paul has already said that if Christ be not risen the preaching is vain, the faith is vain, and the dead in Christ have perished. The sheaf is in. The field is promised.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): Firstfruits of them that slept, Christ risen as the first instalment of the harvest of the dead, pledging and patterning the bodily resurrection of His people.

scriptures: But now is Christ risen from the dead, and become the firstfruits of them that slept.
But every man in his own order: Christ the firstfruits; afterward they that are Christ's at his coming.
And if Christ be not raised, your faith is vain; ye are yet in your sins.

Speak unto the children of Israel, and say unto them, When ye be come into the land which I give unto you, and shall reap the harvest thereof, then ye shall bring a sheaf of the firstfruits of your harvest unto the priest:
corruption_summary: The resurrection is reduced to a symbol of renewal or of the disciples' recovered courage; Paul makes it the first sheaf of a bodily harvest and stakes everything on its being literal.
corruption_paragraphs: The dominant liberal account, from Schleiermacher through Bultmann to the present, treats the resurrection as the rise of Easter faith in the disciples rather than an event in the tomb, and so as a symbol of renewal, of hope, or of the persistence of Jesus' cause. Paul forecloses it in the same chapter: if Christ be not raised, your faith is vain, ye are yet in your sins, and the dead have perished. He does not offer the symbolic reading as a devotional alternative; he calls the preaching of it vain and the apostles false witnesses.

The second corruption is the over-spiritualised evangelical hope that expects a disembodied immortality rather than a raised body, so that funerals speak of a soul in heaven and never of a grave that will open. The firstfruits figure forbids it. A sheaf of grain is the same substance as the harvest it precedes, and Christ rose in a body that could be handled and could eat. Those who are Christ's at His coming will rise as He rose, and this corruptible will put on incorruption.

pos: n. (the gospel's effect upon those who perish)
etymology: Greek osme thanatou, the smell or odour of death, from osme, a fragrance or smell, and thanatos, death. The Authorized Version's savour renders scent rather than taste. The phrase occurs once.
biblical_def: The savour of death is the gospel's effect upon those who reject it, and Paul sets it in deliberate parallel with its opposite: “To the one we are the savour of death unto death; and to the other the savour of life unto life. And who is sufficient for these things?” (2 Corinthians 2:16). The figure comes from the verse before, where the apostles are a sweet savour of Christ unto God, in them that are saved and in them that perish — the same fragrance, two opposite effects. Behind it stands the Roman triumph, where incense was burned along the route: to the victors the smoke meant home and honour, and to the captives walking behind the chariot it meant execution. The preaching does not change according to its audience. One message, faithfully delivered, hardens and saves, and Paul does not treat the hardening as a failure of method. He treats it as the solemn weight of the office and asks who is sufficient for it. The doctrine is the twofold effect of the word and the sovereignty of God in it. The same sun that melts wax hardens clay, and a minister who has grasped this will neither flatter himself when men believe nor adjust the message when they do not.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): Savour of death, the odour of death; the gospel's effect upon them that perish, set against the savour of life unto life in them that are saved.
webster_full: Greek osme, a smell, a fragrance, an odour.
Greek thanatos, death; osme thanatou, the savour of death.
The Authorized Version's savour here means scent, not taste.
Set against the savour of life unto life, 2 Corinthians 2:16.
Drawn from the incense of a Roman triumph, 2 Corinthians 2:14.
scriptures: To the one we are the savour of death unto death; and to the other the savour of life unto life. And who is sufficient for these things?
For we are unto God a sweet savour of Christ, in them that are saved, and in them that perish:
Now thanks be unto God, which always causeth us to triumph in Christ, and maketh manifest the savour of his knowledge by us in every place.
For the preaching of the cross is to them that perish foolishness; but unto us which are saved it is the power of God.
corruption_summary: Preaching is judged by its reception, so that a message which hardens anyone is presumed defective; Paul says the same savour does both and asks who is sufficient.
corruption_paragraphs: The pragmatic corruption is to treat response as the measure of faithfulness. If hearers are offended, the delivery is blamed, the doctrine softened, the hard sayings postponed; the implied principle is that a truly gracious gospel could not harden anybody. Paul's account is the reverse. He is a sweet savour of Christ unto God in them that perish as much as in them that are saved, which means his faithfulness is measured upward and not by the audience. The modern market test would have retired him.

The opposite corruption is the harsh ministry that takes pleasure in giving offence and reads every rejection as proof of fidelity. The question that closes the verse forbids it: who is sufficient for these things? The man who can speak of being a savour of death to his neighbours without trembling has not understood the office. The dictionary holds that the twofold effect is God's doing, that the preacher is responsible for faithfulness and not for outcomes, and that the right posture under this doctrine is the one Paul takes — awe, and a sense of insufficiency.

pos: n. (the narrow entrance into life, which few find)
etymology: From the archaic English strait, narrow, confined, from Latin strictus, drawn tight — not the modern straight, meaning unbent. Rendering Greek stene pule, from stenos, narrow. Named twice.
biblical_def: The strait gate is the narrow entrance into life, and the first thing to settle is the spelling. Strait means narrow or confined, from the Latin strictus, drawn tight — the same word in straitened circumstances and the Strait of Gibraltar. It has nothing to do with straight, meaning unbent, and a reader who confuses them loses the whole figure. Our Lord commands the entering: “Enter ye in at the strait gate: for wide is the gate, and broad is the way, that leadeth to destruction, and many there be which go in thereat” (Matthew 7:13), and then states the contrast: “Because strait is the gate, and narrow is the way, which leadeth unto life, and few there be that find it” (Matthew 7:14). Four contrasts are drawn in two verses — the gate narrow or wide, the way narrow or broad, the end life or destruction, the travellers few or many. In Luke the command is sharper still: “Strive to enter in at the strait gate: for many, I say unto you, will seek to enter in, and shall not be able” (Luke 13:24). A narrow gate admits one at a time and admits nothing carried. It cannot be entered in a crowd, by inheritance, or with baggage, and our Lord says plainly that the majority do not go that way.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): Strait gate, a narrow gate; from strait, narrow or confined, not straight, unbent. Our Lord's figure for the narrow entrance into life, found by few.
webster_full: Archaic English strait, narrow, confined, from Latin strictus, drawn tight.
Not the modern straight, meaning unbent or direct.
The same root gives straitened, strict, and the Strait of Gibraltar.
Rendering Greek stene pule, from stenos, narrow.
Named in Matthew 7:13-14 and Luke 13:24.

corruption_summary: The word is read as straight, and the doctrine of a narrow way found by few is softened into a recommendation of moral uprightness or of many paths up one mountain.
corruption_paragraphs: The commonest error is the simple misreading of strait as straight, which converts a statement about how few enter into a platitude about keeping to the straight and narrow. The deeper corruption is religious pluralism, which cannot allow the verse to mean what it says and so reads the narrow gate as one valid route among many, or as a symbol of sincerity in whatever path a man chooses. Our Lord forecloses this in the same discourse and elsewhere states it without figure: I am the way, the truth, and the life; no man cometh unto the Father, but by me.

The opposite corruption is the sectarian misuse, in which the few who find it are identified with one's own narrow party, and the gate's narrowness becomes a flattering proof of election. The text gives no warrant for that comfort either. Luke's form of the saying is addressed to men who will seek to enter and shall not be able, and the command is strive. The narrowness of the gate is a reason for urgency about oneself, not for satisfaction about one's company.
